why_popular: Cooler, sharper mint for tea and mocktails; a different flavour from chutney pudina
care_tip: Keep it in its own wide pot and repot every year; trim flowering stems to keep leaves coming

why_popular: Daisy-like flowers dried for calming bedtime tea; a cool-season annual for North and Central Indian winters
care_tip: Surface-sow the tiny seeds without covering; pick flowers when fully open and dry them in shade

why_popular: The purple scent of Kashmir's 'purple revolution' fields; in the plains it needs a sunny, dry corner
care_tip: Use sandy, gritty soil in a terracotta pot and water sparingly; it rots in a humid monsoon, so keep it under cover

why_popular: Fragrant leaf offered in pooja and woven into gajras in Maharashtra and Rajasthan; also a mild oregano for cooking
care_tip: Pinch tips to keep it dense and let the soil dry slightly between waterings

why_popular: Silver-green scented leaf offered to Lord Shiva and used in Karnataka and Maharashtra garlands; source of a prized perfume oil
care_tip: A winter crop: sow in October and pick sprigs from January; avoid wet feet

why_popular: Its roots cool summer khus curtains and matka water; deep roots stop soil erosion and filter water
care_tip: Use a deep pot or grow bag for the long roots; trim leaves to 30 cm once a year and use a few roots to scent drinking water

why_popular: An Ayurvedic spice in trikatu and cough remedies; a creeping shade-lover that suits a humid balcony
care_tip: Keep the soil moist and the plant in bright shade; pick the catkins when they turn from green to dark and dry them

why_popular: The famously bitter Ayurvedic herb used for fever and immunity; quick to grow from seed in the monsoon
care_tip: Sow at the start of the monsoon; harvest the whole plant just as flowers appear and dry it in shade

why_popular: The 'king of hair' in Ayurveda; its leaf is the base of bhringraj hair oil and it grows like a weed in damp soil
care_tip: Keep it wet, it loves soggy corners; pick leaves often and it keeps branching

why_popular: The 'renewing' herb of Ayurveda used in kidney and liver tonics; a trailing plant with tiny pink flowers
care_tip: Let it trail from a hanging pot; it is drought-hardy, so water only when the top soil is dry

why_popular: Often sold as 'brahmi' in South India; round leaves eaten in thambuli and chutneys as a memory tonic
care_tip: Grow in a wide shallow pot that never dries out; runners root on their own, so pinch them off to share

why_popular: Grandmother's kidney-stone remedy; new plants sprout from the edges of a single fallen leaf
care_tip: Lay a leaf on moist soil and watch baby plants appear; it spreads easily, so pull extra seedlings

why_popular: A classic Indian medicinal plant behind early blood-pressure drugs; small pink-white flowers and glossy red berries
care_tip: Partial shade and humus-rich, moist soil suit it; never use its root without a doctor's advice

why_popular: Leaves are boiled for joint-pain fomentation and kept in grain bins against insects; a tough, lilac-flowered shrub
care_tip: Prune after flowering to keep it a dense screen; it takes heat and drought once settled

why_popular: The 'bone-setter' of folk medicine; a square-stemmed succulent vine that climbs a railing with tendrils

why_popular: Children's favourite: the leaves fold up the moment you touch them, and it has pink pom-pom flowers too

why_popular: Its flowers and leaves are offered to Lord Shiva and Hanuman, especially in Shravan; host plant of the plain tiger butterfly

why_popular: Offered to Lord Ganesha in bunches of 21; a tray of it gives you fresh durva for every Sankashti and Ganeshotsav

why_popular: Fresh leaves are ground for wedding and Karva Chauth mehendi; tiny flowers have a strong night fragrance
care_tip: Clip it like a hedge to get lots of young leaves; the best colour comes from leaves picked in summer

why_popular: A classic Ayurvedic brain tonic; a small trailing plant with white-pink conch-shaped flowers
care_tip: Sandy, well-drained soil and full sun; let it trail over the pot edge and water only when dry

why_popular: Chewing one leaf stops you tasting sugar for a while; a woody Ayurvedic climber linked to blood-sugar remedies
care_tip: Give it a trellis and pinch the tips to branch; try the leaf trick before eating something sweet

why_popular: Its name means 'diamond teeth': twigs were used as toothbrushes and in herbal tooth powders; yellow flowers in the monsoon
care_tip: Spiny stems make it a good low hedge; trim after flowering and water lightly

why_popular: A Rajasthani and Gujarati staple sabzi that thrives in heat where most beans give up
care_tip: Sow in summer or the monsoon; pick pods young and tender every two days

why_popular: Tender pods and leaves cooked across India; a legume that adds nitrogen to your potting soil

why_popular: Pods grow 40-50 cm long; a monsoon favourite in Odisha, Bengal, Kerala and Chhattisgarh

why_popular: The winter sem of the North and the val papdi of Gujarat's undhiyu; purple flowers climb a balcony in weeks

why_popular: Four-winged pods of the North-East and Kerala; almost every part, from leaves to flowers to tubers, is edible

why_popular: Beloved in Bihar, UP and Bengal; a perennial vine grown from root cuttings that crops for years

why_popular: Little striped tondli for Maharashtrian bhaji and Konkani dishes; one perennial vine fruits most of the year
care_tip: Grow from a stem cutting of a fruiting (female) plant; it can take over a railing, so trim it every month

why_popular: Long gourd for South Indian kootu and Maharashtrian padwal bhaji; lace-like white flowers open at night

why_popular: Source of Agra's petha sweet and South Indian avial; the fruits store for months on a shelf
care_tip: A terrace crop: it needs a big pot and strong support or room to sprawl; keep two or three fruits per vine

why_popular: Sweet-sour kaddu sabzi, bharit and sambar: grown from a few seeds of a store pumpkin; leaves and flowers are edible too
care_tip: Hand-pollinate early in the morning with a male flower if fruits drop; let it sprawl on a terrace floor or trellis

why_popular: Tender gilki sabzi when young; leave one to dry and it becomes a natural loofah scrubber

why_popular: A short-season monsoon delicacy that sells at high prices; it grows back every year from its tuber
care_tip: Grow from a tuber and plant a male with the females; the tuber rests underground through winter

why_popular: Punjabi and Rajasthani summer staple; small round gourds that suit a grow bag on a sunny terrace
care_tip: Pick fruits at tennis-ball size; mulch the bag to keep roots cool in May

why_popular: An exotic sabzi now in every city supermarket; one bush plant gives lots of fruit in North Indian winters

why_popular: A winter superfood that grows well in pots in North and Central India; side shoots keep coming after the main head

why_popular: Kashmir's monji and a quick winter vegetable in Bengal and Maharashtra; bulbs are ready in about 50 days

why_popular: Punjabi shalgam sabzi and winter pickle; both roots and greens are eaten and it is ready in about 50 days
care_tip: Thin seedlings to 10 cm apart; pull roots at 5-8 cm across for the sweetest taste

why_popular: India is the world's second-largest onion grower; in pots it is grown mostly for green leaves and small bulbs

why_popular: Quick Asian green for stir-fries and noodles; baby leaves are ready in four weeks in a shallow tray

why_popular: A cut-and-come-again superfood leaf that grows well in Indian winters; close cousin of Kashmiri haak
care_tip: Pick the lower leaves and leave the top crown growing; leaves turn sweeter after cold nights

why_popular: Rainbow-stemmed spinach beet that keeps giving leaves all winter; looks as good as an ornamental
care_tip: Snip outer leaves at the base and the centre keeps producing for months

why_popular: Winter raita, paratha and saag green of North India; often a free 'weed' that self-sows in pots
care_tip: Scatter seeds in October and pinch the tops for a bushier plant; cook it rather than eating it raw

why_popular: Roast-it-on-coals bhutta: a few plants in a large grow bag give cobs in under three months

why_popular: Assam and Nagaland's famous chilli, once the hottest in the world; one bush gives enough to pickle for a year

why_popular: Leaves for Maharashtrian alu vadi and Gujarati patra, corms for arbi sabzi; the big leaves look tropical on a balcony

why_popular: Diwali suran sabzi in UP and Bihar and a fasting food in Maharashtra; one corm grows a single dramatic umbrella leaf

why_popular: A heat-loving spinach for summer and monsoon when palak fails; fleshy leaves for Bengali and Konkan cooking
care_tip: Grow it up a railing and pinch the tips for curry; cuttings root in water in a few days

why_popular: Bengal and Assam's quick-growing saag; it even grows in a bucket of water on a sunny balcony

why_popular: Sambar's chow chow in South India and the iskus of Darjeeling and the North-East; one fruit sprouts into a huge vine

why_popular: Peppery salad rocket, related to the taramira oil crop of Rajasthan; baby leaves are ready in three weeks
care_tip: Sow a pinch every two weeks for a steady supply; it turns bitter and bolts as the heat rises

why_popular: Mild onion stalk for soups and noodles; grows in North Indian and hill winters in a deep pot

why_popular: The sweet brown fruit of Dahanu and Gujarat; grafted dwarf plants fruit in a large pot within two to three years

why_popular: The purple summer fruit of every Indian childhood; grafted varieties now fruit in big containers

why_popular: Nagpur's famous santra; a grafted mandarin fruits in a big pot and fills the balcony with blossom scent

why_popular: The juice-stall fruit of every Indian street; grafted plants fruit within two to three years in a large pot

why_popular: The lucky 'golden orange' gifted at festivals and housewarmings; a neat little tree loaded with tiny eat-the-peel fruits

why_popular: Grow it free from the leafy top of a market pineapple; one fruit after about two years, plus pups for more

why_popular: Summer's favourite; small 'sugar baby' types fit a terrace grow bag and fruit in about 90 days
care_tip: Choose a small-fruited variety and let it sprawl; stop watering a week before harvest for sweeter fruit

why_popular: Fragrant summer melon of North Indian riverbeds; climbs a trellis if you sling the fruits in a net

why_popular: Muzaffarpur's shahi litchi is GI-tagged; air-layered plants can fruit in a big container where winters are cool and dry

why_popular: Sweet-sour stars sold with chaat masala outside schools; a compact tree that fruits several times a year

why_popular: Very sour finger-like fruits growing straight off the trunk; a Kerala and Goa favourite for fish curry and pickle

why_popular: Tiny purple berries that make the classic North Indian summer sharbat; a bushy shrub kept small by yearly pruning

why_popular: The Konkan's souring agent for solkadhi and the base of cooling kokum sharbat; a slow evergreen tree

why_popular: Crunchy, juicy bell-shaped fruit from Bengal and the Konkan; red Thai varieties are now in every nursery

why_popular: One of the richest sources of vitamin C; a bonsai-like bush that fruits several times a year in a pot

why_popular: Golden berries wrapped in a papery lantern, sold in winter markets of North India; easy from seed in a pot

why_popular: Spring fruit of Punjab, Himachal and the North-East; a handsome large-leaved evergreen that fruits in a big pot

why_popular: Double leaves for Thai curries and soups; a compact citrus grown more for its leaves than its fruit

why_popular: Kerala's state fruit and the kathal sabzi of the North; early-bearing dwarf grafts now fruit in very large containers

why_popular: The long-stemmed show rose of bouquets and flower shows; grafted plants are sold in every nursery

why_popular: A small pot rose that fits a windowsill and flowers in flushes almost all year

why_popular: Its intensely fragrant golden flowers are offered in temples and worn in hair across Maharashtra and the South
care_tip: Grafted plants bloom in a large pot within two years; mulch and keep the soil moist in summer

why_popular: Tiny star flowers that keep their scent for days after falling; strung into garlands and grown near temples
care_tip: Slow but tough: prune it into a dense bush in a big pot and collect the fallen flowers each morning

why_popular: The small, bushy marigold of balcony boxes; a classic companion that keeps nematodes and some pests away from vegetables

why_popular: A cut flower grown widely around Pune and Bengaluru for garlands and bouquets; cheerful pom-poms in winter
care_tip: Sow in September for winter flowers; stake taller types and avoid wetting the leaves in the evening

why_popular: A carpet of bright winter colour in North Indian gardens and pots; cheap and easy from seed

why_popular: Kids love squeezing the 'dragon mouth' flowers; tall spikes in every North Indian winter flower show

why_popular: Towering spikes of hibiscus-like flowers in North Indian spring; the flowers are used in Unani medicine

why_popular: Blue, pink and white winter spikes that bees love; a cottage-garden favourite in North India

why_popular: The most fragrant winter flower of North Indian gardens; a light climber for a sunny railing

why_popular: Silky red and pink winter blooms for North Indian gardens; this is the legal ornamental poppy, not the opium poppy
care_tip: Scatter the tiny seeds on the surface of the final pot; it does not survive being moved

why_popular: Neat clusters of white and pink flowers for winter borders and small pots
care_tip: Sow in autumn and trim lightly after the first flush for a second round

why_popular: A honey-scented white carpet that spills over pot edges and pulls in tiny beneficial insects that eat aphids
care_tip: Plant at the edge of vegetable pots to attract hoverflies; shear back by half if it gets leggy

why_popular: Clove-scented winter spikes that perfume a balcony in the evenings

why_popular: A bouquet flower grown in Pune and Bengaluru polyhouses; spicy-scented blooms in pots in winter

why_popular: Glossy daisies in purple, white and orange that open with the sun; a modern nursery favourite for winter pots
care_tip: Water only when the top soil dries and deadhead often; it rests in the summer heat

why_popular: Striking striped daisies that love hot, dry sun; great for a south-facing ledge where little else survives

why_popular: One of the few plants that flowers non-stop in shade; perfect for north-facing balconies and hanging baskets

why_popular: A shiny-leaved little begonia that flowers all year in bright shade; a staple of hanging baskets
care_tip: Let the top soil dry slightly between waterings; pinch leggy stems to keep it compact

why_popular: The classic window-box flower of hill stations; bright red clusters through winter in the plains
care_tip: Water only when the soil is dry and keep it under a ledge in the monsoon; take cuttings in October

why_popular: India's best-selling orchid: long-lasting flower sprays, and easy in humid cities like Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai
care_tip: Grow it in bark or coconut husk, not soil; water when the medium is nearly dry and feed weak orchid fertiliser weekly

why_popular: The orchid of gifting: one spike stays in flower for two to three months on a bright indoor table
care_tip: Bright indirect light only; water when the bark is dry and the roots look silvery, then drain fully

why_popular: Orchids of the North-East forests; grown with bare roots in hanging baskets in very humid cities
care_tip: Hang it in a slatted basket in bright light and mist the roots once or twice a day in dry weather

why_popular: A bright red or yellow star that lasts for months indoors; a popular gift and office-desk plant
care_tip: Keep a little water in the central cup and the mix just damp; after flowering, grow on the pups

why_popular: Big bold bulbs that flower in about 10 weeks; sold every autumn by Indian bulb sellers for winter pots
care_tip: Plant bulbs 15 cm deep in autumn; very toxic to cats, so skip it if you have one

why_popular: Huge trumpet flowers from a single bulb; a reliable, easy bloomer for Indian balconies every spring
care_tip: Plant with the bulb's neck above the soil; reduce water in winter and it blooms when warmth returns

why_popular: Flame-coloured state flower of Tamil Nadu; a monsoon climber from a tuber
care_tip: Every part is highly poisonous: grow it out of reach of children and pets and wash your hands after handling the tuber

why_popular: Tall florist spikes grown from corms each winter; a favourite for weddings and temple decoration
care_tip: Plant corms every two weeks from October for a long show; stake the spikes

why_popular: Each flower lasts a day but new ones keep coming; a tough, low-maintenance clump for a sunny ledge
care_tip: Divide the clump every three years; very toxic to cats

why_popular: Tropical parrot-beak flowers loved in Kerala and Goa gardens; they last for weeks in a vase
care_tip: Rich moist soil and humidity keep it flowering; cut old stems to the ground after they bloom

why_popular: The 'crane flower' of upmarket gardens and hotel lobbies; slow but stunning in a big pot
care_tip: It flowers only when a little root-bound and in full sun; feed monthly and be patient for 2-3 years

why_popular: Butterfly-shaped white flowers with a heavenly evening scent; very popular in Maharashtra and Kerala
care_tip: It loves wet soil: stand the pot in a tray of water in summer and cut spent stems at the base

why_popular: Curled shrimp-like bracts that sunbirds visit; it flowers almost all year in bright shade
care_tip: Pinch the tips after each flush to stop it getting leggy

why_popular: Sky-blue flower clusters for most of the year; a tough hedge shrub of Indian housing societies
care_tip: Cut it back by half in February to keep it compact; flowers form on new growth

why_popular: Big pink or white bracts that look like paper; a showpiece shrub of South Indian gardens
care_tip: Prune hard in late winter for a compact plant covered in bracts by summer

why_popular: Orange-red tubular flowers that sunbirds and butterflies visit all day; a very heat-tolerant hedge shrub
care_tip: Prune in spring; it is happiest in full sun and needs little water once rooted

why_popular: Small red star flowers on a neat shrub all year; one of the most planted ornamentals in Indian housing societies
care_tip: Very drought-tolerant; all parts, especially the seeds, are poisonous, so avoid it where small children play

why_popular: Fluffy red powder-puff flowers that draw sunbirds; a fine-leaved shrub for a large terrace pot
care_tip: Trim after flowering to keep it bushy; the leaves fold up at night

why_popular: The daytime partner of raat ki rani: small white flowers scent the balcony during the day
care_tip: Prune after each flush to keep it bushy; the berries are toxic, so pick them off if kids are around

why_popular: Creamy white flowers with a rich scent, offered in pooja and worn in hair in Bengal and the South
care_tip: It likes slightly acidic soil: add used tea leaves or coffee grounds and keep it evenly moist; yellow leaves mean it needs iron

why_popular: Flowers open purple, fade to lavender, then white: three colours on one bush, with a sweet scent
care_tip: Bright shade and moist, rich soil; the whole plant is poisonous to dogs

why_popular: Blazing orange daisies that butterflies cannot resist; it thrives in summer heat when other annuals fade
care_tip: Sow straight into a big pot in the sunniest spot; deadhead and it flowers for months

why_popular: True-blue winter flowers that bees love; easy from seed in North and Central India
care_tip: Sow directly in October; the petals are edible and look great scattered on salads

why_popular: Sunny yellow daisies that keep flowering in heat and poor soil; a bee and butterfly magnet
care_tip: Don't overfeed, as lean soil gives more flowers; deadhead weekly

why_popular: Golden daisies with dark centres for late winter and spring; long-lasting in a vase
care_tip: Sow in autumn and deadhead often; avoid watering the leaves to prevent mildew

why_popular: A tough groundcover with small yellow daisies all year; often used to cover bare soil in large planters
care_tip: Keep it in a pot of its own as it spreads aggressively; never dump cuttings on open ground

why_popular: A dome of blue, purple and pink daisies for shady winter balconies in North India
care_tip: Keep it out of afternoon sun and evenly moist; it finishes as the heat comes in March

why_popular: Big mop-head flowers of Shillong, Ooty and Darjeeling; blooms turn blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline
care_tip: Best in hill cities or cool, shady balconies; never let it wilt, and give it morning sun only

why_popular: An evergreen climber with masses of scented white stars in spring; neater than true jasmines on a grill
care_tip: Tie young stems to the grill; trim after flowering to keep it dense

why_popular: Flowers open around 4 pm and scent the evening; it self-sows in Indian village courtyards
care_tip: Easy from its black seeds; it forms a tuber and returns each year, but the seeds and roots are poisonous

why_popular: Huge white flowers that unfurl at dusk with a sweet scent; a magical evening climber for a railing
care_tip: Nick and soak the seeds overnight; sit nearby at sunset to watch the flowers open

why_popular: A glossy-leaved climber with big pink and red trumpets; a modern nursery favourite for grills and obelisks
care_tip: Water when the top soil dries and feed every two weeks in summer; the sap is irritating

why_popular: Cheerful orange and yellow flowers with dark eyes; a light, quick climber for a sunny or half-shaded grill
care_tip: Give it strings or a net to twine on; trim lightly to keep it flowering

why_popular: White lantern bracts with red flowers peeping out; a neat climber for bright shade
care_tip: Prune after flowering and keep it out of hot afternoon sun

why_popular: The leaves smell of garlic and lavender flowers smother the vine twice a year; popular on Indian compound walls
care_tip: Give it strong support and prune after each flowering to keep it from turning woody

why_popular: Clouds of pink flowers that bees swarm over; one of the toughest, fastest covers for a hot wall
care_tip: Very vigorous: cut it back hard each winter and don't let seeds escape into wild land

why_popular: Sheets of orange tubular flowers in winter on Indian bungalow walls and gates; loved by sunbirds
care_tip: It needs a big pot and a strong wall or pergola; prune after flowering in March

why_popular: Feathery leaves and tiny red stars that sunbirds visit; called Ganesh vel in Maharashtra
care_tip: Sow seeds right at the base of a string or grill; it self-sows every year after

why_popular: Hanging clusters of pale-blue trumpets that carpenter bees visit all day; a lively shade vine
care_tip: It grows huge: prune every few months and give it a very strong pergola

why_popular: Long purple sprays like a tropical wisteria; spectacular on gates in spring
care_tip: Slow to settle but long-lived; feed and water well in its first two years

why_popular: Green flowers that turn yellow and smell like ripe fruit; an old favourite of temple and bungalow gardens in Maharashtra and the South
care_tip: It climbs with hooks, so train it on a strong grill; you'll find the hidden flowers by their scent

why_popular: The nargis of Kashmir and Urdu poetry; fragrant white clusters from bulbs in cool North Indian winters
care_tip: Plant bulbs in November with the tips just under the soil; keep it cool and stop watering when the leaves yellow

why_popular: Big spidery white flowers with a night scent; grown near homes and temples and used in folk remedies
care_tip: A very tough bulb that tolerates wet soil and heat; the bulb is poisonous

why_popular: Crinkled pink, mauve and white flowers all summer; a small cousin of Tamhan, Maharashtra's state flower
care_tip: Prune in February, since flowers come on new shoots; it drops its leaves briefly in winter

why_popular: Red brushes that sunbirds and bees love; a tough evergreen screen for a hot, windy terrace
care_tip: Prune lightly just after flowering; the crushed leaves smell of lemon

why_popular: The sacred tree under which Sita waited in Lanka; orange flower clusters in spring and a famous Ayurvedic bark
care_tip: This is not the tall 'false Ashok' of avenues; it likes partial shade and moist soil and grows slowly in a big pot

why_popular: Red bracts that peak at Christmas; sold in pots across India in December and grown as shrubs in Bengaluru and Shillong

why_popular: Sky-blue flowers on a silver-green mound, now in every Indian nursery; perfect along a sunny railing box

why_popular: Bright yellow flowers that open mid-morning and close by afternoon; it self-sows and keeps flowering all year

why_popular: Purple and pink spikes that keep flowering through Indian summers when snapdragons can't

why_popular: Elegant white or coloured spathes for bouquets; best in hill cities and cool, shady balconies
care_tip: Keep the soil moist and the pot in morning sun; all parts are toxic if eaten

why_popular: Giant plate-sized flowers in sunset colours; the collector's hibiscus of Indian nursery shows

why_popular: The 'brahma kamal' of Indian homes (the Himalayan one is a different plant): its huge white flower opens for one night with a powerful scent and families stay up to watch

why_popular: State flower of Maharashtra: big mauve-pink flower sprays in summer on a small deciduous tree

why_popular: Its orange flowers once made natural Holi colour and it is the state flower of Jharkhand; the leaves make traditional pattals

why_popular: Tall red flower spikes on banana-like leaves; a Kerala and Goa garden favourite for shady corners

why_popular: The evergreen white temple champa with a rich scent; offered to deities across Maharashtra and the South

why_popular: Silver-speckled velvety leaves; a slower, more decorative cousin of the money plant for shelves and hanging pots

why_popular: Deeply cut, glossy leaves on a compact clump; popular in Indian apartment lobbies and big balcony corners
care_tip: Bright shade and moderate water; wipe the leaves monthly to keep them glossy

why_popular: White pinstriped leaves that made it an Instagram favourite; now sold by most Indian online nurseries

why_popular: Leaves full of holes on a fast trailing or climbing vine; a modern favourite for moss poles and hanging pots

why_popular: Huge upright arrow leaves for a tropical look; grows fast in humid Indian summers

why_popular: Dark arrow leaves with bright white veins; a striking table plant for a bright room

why_popular: Paper-thin heart leaves splashed in pink, red and white; brightens shady balconies through the monsoon

why_popular: Leaves fold up at night like hands in prayer; patterned foliage for a bright bathroom or shaded window

why_popular: Tiny leaves with bright pink or white veins; the go-to plant for terrariums and small desks

why_popular: Pink- or white-speckled leaves that brighten a windowsill; cheap and quick from seed or cutting

why_popular: Round coin-like leaves on a neat little plant; gifted for luck and endlessly shared as pups

why_popular: Silver-painted leaves for a shady shelf; easy, quick to root and very forgiving

why_popular: A tall, low-light tree for an office or living-room corner; sold as 'fortune plant' or 'mass cane'

why_popular: Dense rosettes of dark glossy leaves; one of the toughest plants for a dim corner

why_popular: Bold red, pink and purple sword leaves; often sold as 'red dracaena' for balcony colour

why_popular: An elegant small-leaved tree for an indoor corner or balcony; also the classic Indian bonsai starter

why_popular: The fat-rooted 'ginseng ficus' sold as a ready bonsai in every Indian nursery and mall

why_popular: A slow, elegant fan palm that copes with low light and AC rooms; a NASA clean-air study favourite

why_popular: A small, soft palm for tables and dim corners; one of the safest palms around pets

why_popular: Leaflets shaped like fish fins; a clumping tropical palm for big pots on shaded terraces

why_popular: A living fossil with stiff, glossy fronds; a long-lived showpiece in Indian bungalow gardens

why_popular: A swollen 'elephant foot' trunk topped with a fountain of thin leaves; it stores water and forgives neglect

why_popular: Big round fan leaves that droop at the tips; a slow, tough palm for sunny or shaded terraces

why_popular: Wavy, glossy fronds in a nest-like rosette; a fern that doesn't drop leaves everywhere

why_popular: Delicate black-stemmed fronds like those growing wild on damp Western Ghats walls; lovely in a shady bathroom

why_popular: Round, spear-like leaves often sold braided; just as tough as the classic snake plant

why_popular: Deep purple trailing stems with tiny pink flowers; one of the cheapest, toughest balcony plants

why_popular: A braided trunk with lucky five-leaf hands; a Vastu and feng shui gift for new homes and offices

why_popular: Grows with no soil at all; sold glued to driftwood, shells and hanging globes

why_popular: Classic trailing ivy for hill homes and cool, shady Indian balconies; a good wall and basket plant

why_popular: Tiny leaves that stick flat to walls; it covers a bare balcony wall in green and cools it

why_popular: Lacy or round-leaved shrubs sold in every Indian nursery for hedges, pots and bonsai

why_popular: Copper, red and green mottled leaves for hedges and colourful pots; it loves heat

why_popular: The most common clipped hedge in Indian colonies and parks; it takes salt wind, heat and heavy pruning

why_popular: Dark-green grassy tufts for edging, between stepping stones or under bigger pots in shade

why_popular: Burgundy grass with feathery plumes that sway in the breeze; a modern terrace accent

why_popular: The soft lawn of Indian terraces and society gardens; a tray of it gives a barefoot green patch on a balcony

why_popular: A soft, round green bush that turns fiery red in autumn; quick from seed in summer

why_popular: Purple-backed sword leaves in a neat clump; one of the most common balcony plants in Mumbai and Kerala

why_popular: Silver, pink and maroon painted leaves; the showiest foliage for a bright, humid shelf

why_popular: Angel-wing leaves with silver spots and red undersides; a hot favourite of Indian plant Instagram

why_popular: Butterfly-shaped purple leaves that fold up at night; tiny pink flowers most of the year

why_popular: The red, yellow and green 'rangoli plant' used to write names and patterns in Indian public gardens

why_popular: Chikmagalur's famous crop, grown at home as a glossy indoor shrub with jasmine-scented flowers and red cherries

why_popular: Waxy leaves and star-shaped porcelain flowers with a sweet night scent; a slow trailing collector's plant

why_popular: Flat pads with fuzzy dots that look like rabbit ears; a cute, sun-loving cactus for a dry ledge

why_popular: A perfect golden ball of spines; the iconic cactus of Indian succulent shops

why_popular: A spineless forest cactus that flowers pink and red in winter; grows beautifully in hanging pots

why_popular: Neon red, orange or yellow cactus balls grafted on a green stem; a popular desk gift

why_popular: Thick, tongue-shaped speckled leaves; one of the best succulents for low light and small pots

why_popular: Pastel grey-pink rosettes that trail over the pot edge; every fallen leaf grows a new plant

why_popular: Fuzzy silver leaves with brown tips like little panda paws; children love touching it

why_popular: Rows of baby plantlets along every leaf edge drop and root on their own; a fun plant for kids to watch

why_popular: Green pencil-thin branches; the 'sher' hedge of Indian villages and a sculptural pot plant

why_popular: Zig-zag stems with variegated leaves and red slipper flowers; a hardy pot and hedge plant

why_popular: Banana-shaped leaves on trailing stems; faster and tougher than string of pearls

why_popular: Spiky architectural leaves that take heat, drought and neglect; good for a hot terrace or office corner

why_popular: Camphor-scented tulsi used against mosquitoes and in steam inhalation; grows into a woody bush

why_popular: The digestive seed in parathas and kadha; tiny white flower umbrellas bring hoverflies in winter

why_popular: The black seed on naan and in pickles; blue starry flowers in North Indian winters

why_popular: The perfume-oil plant grown in Kerala and Assam; velvety leaves smell earthy and sweet when crushed

why_popular: True Ceylon cinnamon from the Western Ghats; the young leaves are also used like bay leaf

why_popular: A rhizome that smells of raw mango; grated into Maharashtrian and Gujarati winter pickles

why_popular: Thai-curry rhizome that is also an old Ayurvedic cough remedy; tall ginger-like leaves

why_popular: Yellow-flowered shrub whose leaves are the herbal laxative sold in every Indian pharmacy

why_popular: Fresh green tur for Gujarati undhiyu and Maharashtrian usal; a perennial shrub that also feeds the soil

why_popular: Green harbhara roasted in winter (hurda-style) and the tender leaves cooked as bhaji

why_popular: The seed of Sankranti's til-gul; foxglove-like flowers in summer and a handful of seeds per plant

why_popular: The orange and yellow cosmos that self-sows in every Indian city; butterflies cover it in the monsoon

why_popular: Classic big white daisies for winter pots in North India and the hills

why_popular: Fluffy blue pom-pom flowers for edging pots; flowers for months and draws butterflies

why_popular: Tall violet-blue spikes that bees adore; tougher in Indian summers than red salvia

why_popular: Fountains of rush-like stems with red tubular flowers; sunbirds visit all day

why_popular: Fiery red-orange crests on a fast shrub; offered in temples and seen in every Indian village

why_popular: Its flower is said to show Krishna, the Pandavas and the Kauravas; a sacred, fragrant railing climber

why_popular: A sweetly scented climber sung of in Sanskrit poetry; frilly white-and-yellow flowers in spring

why_popular: Graceful feathery palm for sunny balconies and entrances; slow and long-lived

why_popular: Long fuzzy red tails hang from this shrub; children love touching them

why_popular: Glossy beet-red leaves for colour in pots and borders; cheap and roots from any cutting

why_popular: The audumbar tree of Shri Datta, worshipped across Maharashtra; figs grow in clusters on the trunk

why_popular: The sacred fragrant wood of pooja and tilak; a semi-parasite that needs a companion plant's roots

why_popular: The tree that gives Shiva's prayer beads; grown as a sacred specimen in big pots in humid cities

why_popular: Krishna's tree from the Bhagavata: golf-ball flowers with a sweet scent in the monsoon

why_popular: Fragrant white flowers with golden stamens used in Ayurveda and temple offerings; red new leaves

why_popular: Spiny Ayurvedic herb in dashamoola and cough remedies; purple flowers and little striped fruits

why_popular: White-flowered native plumbago whose root is a classic Ayurvedic digestive; flowers all year

why_popular: Gives two spices: nutmeg and the red mace around it; grown under coconut palms in Kerala

why_popular: The flower bud spice of every garam masala; a glossy, aromatic tree for humid southern terraces

why_popular: The orchid that gives vanilla pods; grown on support trees in Kerala and Karnataka
